I have three rules and the first one is about order, not about words. Whatever takes the fear away, I say first. Usually that means two sentences: it is not contagious, and it is not cancer. Before that, nothing I say lands. A frightened patient is not listening to your explanation, they are waiting for the sentence they are afraid of, and until it arrives they hear nothing else. Second rule. One technical word, at most, and only after the plain version. The plain version is the explanation; the technical word is a label, so they can look it up later and find the right thing. Residents do it backwards. They lead with the label, because the label is what they revised, and then they translate it, and by then the patient has stopped following. And the third rule is the hardest one, which is about the word cure. Never promise one that does not exist. Not softly, not by implication, not by saying we will get rid of this. Patients forgive a hard truth. I have never once seen a patient forgive a promise that failed.

I understood about half of it, and I nodded through all of it. There is one sentence I remember word for word, and it is the one that helped: my skin is building itself too fast. That is the only thing I could repeat to my husband that evening, and honestly it was enough for that first night. What I got wrong was the other word. She said remission and I heard it had gone. So when it came back in the spring I thought either I had done something or the treatment had stopped working, and I very nearly threw the tube away. It took a nurse, on the phone, to tell me that a relapse is part of how this behaves and not a failure. Nobody had told me that, or maybe somebody had and I was not listening yet. And I will tell you the thing I wish she had done. I wish she had asked me whether I had understood. Not explained it again. Just asked. Because I was never going to raise my hand in that room and say no.
